title: Acharei Mot: ask the person first (Mishnah Yoma 8:9)
hook: Yom Kippur atones between people and God, but wrongs between people need their forgiveness

segments.voice: Yesterday, Azazel: the goat that carried the wrongs away. Your line was send it away. Did you tear up that scrap of paper? Today, the catch I promised. Day four hundred eight.

A sharp word at dinner. A man snaps at his brother, says something cruel. Later, alone, he sits quietly, sincerely sorry, and asks God to forgive him. He feels lighter. Done. But his brother is still in the next room, still stung, and nobody has said a word to him. Leviticus 16 promises that on Yom Kippur, the people will be cleansed of all their sins. All of them. The rabbis read that promise very closely, and found a condition hidden in two words.
screen: `SORRY, BUT ONLY TO GOD.` → `HIS BROTHER, STILL STUNG.` → `A CONDITION IN TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. Leviticus 16:30 says that on this day atonement will be made for you, from all your sins, before the Lord. Second, the reading. In the Mishnah, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah leans on those two words: before the Lord. Wrongs between a person and God, he teaches, Yom Kippur atones for. But wrongs between a person and another person, Yom Kippur does not atone for, until you make it right with them. Not even Yom Kippur skips that step. Third, the steps. Maimonides spells it out. Repay what you owe. Go to the person and ask their forgiveness. If they refuse, come back with three friends and try again. Up to three times. If they still refuse, you've done your part, and the burden passes to them. And he adds a word to the one being asked: don't be cruel. When someone sincerely asks, forgive, even if it's hard. Fourth, the season. Because of this teaching, the days before Yom Kippur can fill with phone calls, emails, awkward conversations at the kiddush table. People ask each other, plainly: if I've hurt you this year, I'm sorry, please forgive me. Yesterday's practice tore up a wrong and sent it away. In the Mishnah's terms, that kind of turning belongs to what lies between a person and God. But if the wrong had a person on the other end, the Mishnah is clear about the order. Ask the person first.
screen: `FROM ALL YOUR SINS, BEFORE THE LORD.` · `BETWEEN PEOPLE: MAKE IT RIGHT.` · `UP TO THREE TIMES.` · `THE SEASON OF ASKING.` · then, large: `ASK THE PERSON FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: apologize to someone directly. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person you've wronged, recently or long ago, who has never heard you say sorry for it. Picture their face. Now picture yourself saying it, simply: I'm sorry for what I did. No speech, no excuse, no but. Notice whether that's hard. Then decide when you'll actually say it: today, this week, in a message or in person. The bell holds the time.
Acharei Mot. The portion of the Day of Atonement, and the Mishnah's teaching that wrongs between people need the other person's forgiveness first.
Your line: ask the person first. Today, say sorry to one person you've wronged, directly, without a but. Day four hundred eight.

howItsDone: In the days before Yom Kippur, many Jews ask family, friends and coworkers for forgiveness directly, and some recite a prayer of forgiving others, Tefillah Zakkah, before Kol Nidre.

original.note: Hebrew: "between a person and their fellow": the Mishnah's phrase for wrongs between people.

trapdoor: what you thought: Yom Kippur wipes the slate clean.
what it means: for wrongs against people, you have to go to them first.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 reads 'before the LORD' in Leviticus 16:30 as limiting the day's atonement; Maimonides, Laws of Repentance 2:9–10, sets out the three attempts.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 2:9–10

notes: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 and Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah's derivation from 'before the LORD': confirm.

Maimonides, Teshuvah 2:9 (three times with three people; then the refuser is the sinner) and 2:10 (not to be cruel/hard to appease); confirm. Exception for a teacher (ask even a thousand times) omitted.
Tefillah Zakkah (said by many Ashkenazim before Kol Nidre) includes forgiving others; confirm the howItsDone description.
